legend: There is a hidden positive integer k$$$k$$$ that has exactly n$$$n$$$ divisors. These divisors were put into an array a$$$a$$$ which was then shuffled into a hidden order.

You can ask the interactor questions of the form ? i j, and you will receive the position of gcd(ai,aj)$$$\gcd(a_i, a_j)$$$ in a$$$a$$$. Note that since a$$$a$$$ contains all divisors of k$$$k$$$, this value is guaranteed to exist and be unique.
Using at most 3n$$$3n$$$ queries, determine which indices of a$$$a$$$ contain prime numbers.
input: The input consists of one line containing an integer n$$$n$$$ (1≤n≤104$$$1\leq n\leq 10^4$$$) — the number of divisors of k$$$k$$$.
Note that we make no guarantees about the magnitude of k$$$k$$$.
After reading in n$$$n$$$, you can make up to 3n$$$3n$$$ queries.
For each query, print a line of the form ? i j (1≤i,j≤n$$$1 \le i, j \le n$$$).
After printing the query, you can then read in an integer x$$$x$$$, where ax=gcd(ai,aj)$$$a_x = \gcd(a_i, a_j)$$$.

Once you have determined which indices contain prime numbers, print a single line ! m p_1 p_2 ... p_m (0≤m≤n$$$0 \le m \le n$$$, 1≤pi≤n$$$1 \le p_i \le n$$$, where m$$$m$$$ is the number of prime factors and p1$$$p_1$$$ through pm$$$p_m$$$ are their positions in a$$$a$$$. This is not counted towards your total of 3n$$$3n$$$ queries.
After printing a query do not forget to output the end of line and flush the output. Otherwise, you will get Idleness limit exceeded. To do this, use:
see the documentation for other languages.
The interactor is non-adaptive. This means that the array a$$$a$$$ is fixed at the start of the interaction, and does not change after the queries.
note: In the first test, after the first query, we know that gcd(a2,a4)=a1$$$\gcd(a_2, a_4) = a_1$$$. It can be shown that since n=4$$$n=4$$$, this query result implies that a2$$$a_2$$$ and a4$$$a_4$$$ are the prime factors of k$$$k$$$.

In the second test n=1$$$n=1$$$, and therefore k=1$$$k=1$$$, because 1$$$1$$$ is the only positive integer with only one divisor. Since 1$$$1$$$ has no prime factors, we can simply output ! 0 without making any queries.
